notes: Synonym format with one marked word, but the word is aback inside the fixed phrase taken aback; the meaning comes from the idiom, not from aback alone. Also fits vocabulary.synonyms, whose rule sends a marked idiom to idioms.idioms but is silent when only part of the idiom is marked.

sonnet.detail: Three items in this sample (Q2, Q46, Q56) need prior knowledge of a specific character, object or scene, with no passage text and no This question is based on line. The taxonomy's own definition of comprehension.prescribed-text depends on knowing the passage was not supplied, and the sorting rules for comprehension.factual and comprehension.tone assume an unseen passage was supplied. A question with neither cue attached is genuinely undecidable between prescribed-text and factual or tone from its text alone. A worked fix would be an index of character and setting names per prescribed novel, so a classifier without exam-day context could still route these questions correctly.

The covers line's determiner examples are few, a few, little, a little, much, many, each, every, some, any. It does not mention all, both, whole or neither, though real papers test them directly against each other (Q68: All the guests vs Every of the guests vs The whole guests; Q72: whether both/either/each/neither Ola and her sister). Both fit the subtopic by function, but a reader checking only the listed examples could reasonably send them to word-classes.nouns instead.

opus.detail: 19 of 80 questions land here, across five different novels (The Life Changer, In Dependence, Sweet Sixteen, The Last Days at Forcados High School, and one with Teacher Bade). A score on this subtopic mixes books a student may never have read and changes meaning every year. It needs a per-title tag (a field, not a subtopic) so practice can be filtered to the current year's novel; three items here (2, 46, 56) name no novel at all and had to be placed by character names.

The rule turns on a recognised confusable pair or set, but recognised is never defined. through, thorough, though (Q74) is a classic taught confusable set yet its gap is decided by which word fits, which the rule sends to vocabulary.word-choice. Give a closed list of confusable sets, or decide by whether the options share most of their spelling.

The rule sends a marked idiom to idioms.idioms but says nothing when only one word of a fixed phrase is marked (taken aback, Q11). Add: when the marked word only has its meaning inside a fixed phrase, place under idioms.idioms.

Compound adjectives, especially number plus noun before a noun (a five-day conference, a ten-year-old boy), have no named home. The singular noun points to word-classes.nouns, the hyphen to mechanics.punctuation (Q28). Name them in one covers line, most naturally adjectives-adverbs, and point the other two there.

The present simple for future time after when, before, until, as soon as (when the rain stops, Q25) is not named. It is a staple item and sits next to verbs.mood-conditionals, whose rule claims any verb in an if clause; state that time clauses go to verbs.tenses.
